title: 1000 Cuts
subtitle: How the Williams family's standing in law was cut down, from the peak to the fall

peak.event: John Williams holds Great House Farm from the Bute estate; a Feb 1916 Bute yearly tenancy with plan names him; the 1904 Bute rent audit lists him "of Llandough Farm".
peak.label: Record
peak.note: The family's long occupation is on record. The same records describe it as a tenancy from Bute, which is the frame the law later used.

peak.event: Marconi's wireless tests at Lavernock and Flat Holm, close by. Family tradition holds that he stayed at the farm.
peak.label: Not yet confirmed
peak.note: The 1897 press and Kemp's diary extracts record the tests but do not name Great House Farm. The stay would be confirmed by the full Kemp diary (Bodleian MS. Marconi 89) or a letter placing the team at the farm.

peak.event: "Peerless" Jim Driscoll's first fight in the farm barn.
peak.label: Not yet confirmed
peak.note: A secondary local-history summary places the fight in the barn; the year and the National Monuments Record citation have not yet been located.

peak.event: Tree planting on Parcel A, the house parcel, as an act of ownership, with the town as witness; the family's acts of occupation.
peak.label: Family testimony
peak.note: Testimony and an undated photograph. Dated photographs, aerial images or survey sheets would confirm the planting and its extent.

peak.event: Last rent for the house parcel paid in 1928, when the quarry machinery left; no rent for the house parcel after that.
peak.label: Family testimony
peak.note: Mary (Nancy) Williams's recollection; the receipt is not located. Cuts against: the Court of Appeal recorded rent arrears in the mid-1930s and late 1940s and a last payment, under a judgment for arrears, in 1953.

peak.event: No one takes issue with the stopped rent for about twenty years, until the 1949 surrender and re-grant.
peak.label: Family testimony
peak.note: Our reading of the family account. The judgment instead records arrears "in the mid-1930s and in the late 1940s" as the reason for the 1949 arrangement.

peak.event: The 1939 Western Ground Rents agreement plan shows the fields (Parcel B) only, highlighted; the house parcel is not shown on it.
peak.label: Record
peak.note: Supports the family's reading that the house parcel stood apart from the let fields. Page 1 of the agreement is not yet held.

cuts.event: Bute grants John Williams a yearly agricultural tenancy of "the whole of the farm", with plan.
cuts.blow: The first paper that names the family as tenants. Every later court began from it: the Court of Appeal opens with Bute letting "the whole of the farm" to John Williams.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: Bute (Mountjoy) sells the reversion to Western Ground Rents Ltd, a ground-rent company; the conveyance later becomes the root of title.
cuts.blow: The landlord the family knew is replaced by a company holding a paper title. From here a written chain runs to BP; the family hold no paper of their own in it.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: The Limitation Act 1939 comes into force: 12 years of adverse possession bars the owner (s.10 possession must be "adverse"; s.13 a formal entry alone keeps nothing alive).
cuts.blow: It set the 12-year test the family would be judged by. Under it, a tenancy, a rent payment, a court action or a licence stops or restarts the clock, so each later step against the family was measured against this Act.
cuts.label: Record (the Act, as applied in the 1987 judgment)

cuts.event: The courts record John Williams as falling into rent arrears.
cuts.blow: In the law's eyes the stopped rent became arrears owed by a tenant, not the end of a tenancy. This is the opposite of the family's 1928 account, and it is the version the court accepted.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: John Williams's tenancy is surrendered and a new yearly agricultural tenancy is granted to his son-in-law Frederick Buckler. It is never put in writing.
cuts.blow: Occupation passed from the Williams line to a yearly tenant, so the family's presence was recast as permission. On our reading this is the first deliberate step to make the occupancy of Parcel A look permissive.
cuts.label: Record (the grant); our reading (its purpose)

cuts.event: Family title papers removed from the farmhouse blanket box.
cuts.blow: The family lost the documents they would later need to prove a title of their own. No court ever saw them.
cuts.label: Family testimony

cuts.event: Frederick Buckler's last rent payment, made under a county-court judgment for arrears.
cuts.blow: A payment under a judgment acknowledged the landlord's title, so no 12-year clock could run before it.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: A further attempt to treat Frederick Buckler as a tenant.
cuts.blow: Another step putting the family's occupation on a tenancy footing.
cuts.label: Not yet confirmed (source pending)

cuts.event: A notice to quit ends Frederick Buckler's tenancy.
cuts.blow: The family were now occupiers with no tenancy. The Court of Appeal later held that Frederick and Mary were in adverse possession of the house and garden from this date, so the clock did start.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: Western Ground Rents obtains a summary possession order (Order 14) in the High Court and enforces it on 4 July 1955: all the farm is taken except the farmhouse and garden.
cuts.blow: The fields were lost in one summary step. The house survived only because Mary had just had a leg amputated and refused to leave. From then on the family held the house alone, against a court order.
cuts.label: Record (the judgment); the order itself is not yet located

cuts.event: Leckwith Common inquiry and Glamorgan County Council acquisitions near the farm; Mary's "Crichel Down" objection goes no further, and no petition is presented in Parliament.
cuts.blow: The land around the house passed into public schemes while her objection had no legal effect. Our reading: it showed the family's word carried no weight with public bodies.
cuts.label: Record (press); our reading (its effect)

cuts.event: Western Ground Rents offers Mary a tenancy of the house and garden; she refuses. Alternative housing is offered and refused.
cuts.blow: The offers built a paper record of the family as would-be tenants. In 1986 the trial judge used the March 1965 offer to find that Frederick had no intention to possess as owner.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: Cardiff County Court possession order for the farmhouse and garden (Judge Temple Morris QC), with mesne profits; a suspended committal order against Frederick Buckler follows in June 1963.
cuts.blow: The decisive cut of the 1960s. Because it came before 12 years had run, the Court of Appeal held the owner's title was never extinguished. The order then lay unused for 12 years and was revived in 1974.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: Frederick Buckler dies. Mary stays in the house.
cuts.blow: The trial judge held that while he lived only his intention counted, so Mary's own clear intention to own was given no effect before his death.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: Western Ground Rents sells the farm, including the farmhouse, to BP Pension Trust.
cuts.blow: A national institution with full legal resources took over the paper title and, as successor, the benefit of the 1962 order.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: Village green VG41 registered by Glamorgan County Council.
cuts.blow: In the family's frame, one of three "synthetic" versions of Parcel A made without the occupier. Cuts against: the certified map shows a small roadside wedge, so this reading is weak on the map read so far.
cuts.label: Record (registration); our reading (its effect) — weakened

cuts.event: Outline planning permission for about 13 houses, with an ownership certificate.
cuts.blow: The owner certified ownership to the planning authority and planned houses on the site. On paper the land was already a development site with the family inside it.
cuts.label: Record (planning register)

cuts.event: BP Pension Trust's new possession action: Mary pleads that BP's claim is barred by adverse possession under the 1939 Act. The action is adjourned part-heard and "has never been finally heard".
cuts.blow: Her plea of ownership was never decided. It still sits undecided on the court file, so it was never won and never lost.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: BP Pension Trust gets leave to execute the 1962 order (Judge Watkin Powell); the warrant may be enforced from 31 Oct 1974. She appeals, saying she had too little notice to be heard.
cuts.blow: A 12-year-old order was revived about 12 weeks before the 12-year period from it ran out (11 Dec 1974), without her being heard.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: Two letters, from BP Pension Trust and BP Properties, sent to her solicitor, allow her to stay rent-free for life: "no proceedings will be commenced until you personally no longer live there".
cuts.blow: The cut the courts rested on. Written without her agreement, the letters made her possession "by the licence of BP Properties", so it was no longer adverse. Her occupation was turned into permission by letter.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: On her solicitors' advice she does nothing while the 12 years from the 1962 order run out, and does not reject the letters.
cuts.blow: The Court of Appeal held that "she did not, however, do that" (reject the letters). Her silence was read as accepting the permission rather than claiming ownership.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: BP Pension Trust conveys the farmhouse plot and other land to BP Properties, reserving 80-year road and sewer rights "to serve any development".
cuts.blow: The house passed to the company that wrote the licence letter, with development rights built into the deed.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: The Vale of Glamorgan becomes a compulsory registration area.
cuts.blow: This brought in the machinery that would turn BP's paper title into a title guaranteed by the state.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: The fields (Parcel B) pass between BP companies and are registered (WA231076), as the law required within two months.
cuts.blow: Background only. It left the farmhouse as the only unregistered piece of the BP farm.
cuts.label: Record (context)

cuts.event: BP Properties applies to register the farmhouse (Form 1C, WA240304) while Mary is alive. A BP officer has to swear BP is in possession. This was BP's only voluntary filing.
cuts.blow: The family home was put on the state register in BP's name, dated as of a day she lived there. BP's "possession" could only be her occupation as its licensee under the 1974 letters.
cuts.label: Record (application, date); our reading (what had to be sworn)

cuts.event: Mary Williams (Mrs Buckler) dies, after an illness in the weeks before (family testimony).
cuts.blow: BP's own undertaking ("until you personally no longer live there") fell away. In BP's own words in 1988, her death was when "it became clear her son was not going to leave".
cuts.label: Record (month); family record (day); testimony (illness)

cuts.event: The Registry examines the farmhouse application after her death: Linklaters letter of 8 Apr (form D23), correspondence of 12 Apr and letters of 12 May 1983.
cuts.blow: The title was completed after she died, but it speaks from a date when she was alive. What the letters told the Registry about who lived there is not yet known; the Registry's copy file (due 28 Oct 2026) would confirm it.
cuts.label: Record (letters exist); our reading (their effect)

cuts.event: The Commons Registration (Glamorgan) Act 1983 validates the Glamorgan common-land registers.
cuts.blow: Parliament confirmed the registers made without the family. Cuts against: the Act covers common land only, not village greens, so on our reading it did not touch VG41 or the farmhouse directly.
cuts.label: Record (the Act); our reading — no direct effect found

cuts.event: BP Properties issues a writ for possession against her son, the occupier.
cuts.blow: The family were now defending, not claiming. The son was sued as an occupier with no licence, and his own 12-year period had barely begun.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: High Court trial in Cardiff; Hollis J gives judgment for BP.
cuts.blow: The first decision on the merits. It held Frederick's possession was not adverse and the letters made Mary a licensee, so the defence under the 1939 and 1980 Acts failed.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: The farmhouse title is merged into the farm title (application, WA231076 item 14) while the appeal is pending.
cuts.blow: The house disappeared into BP's larger title before the appeal was heard. Our reading: if the 1983 title had been possessory, upgrading it while an adverse claim was open was barred from 1 Jan 1987. This is not yet confirmed.
cuts.label: Record (application); our reading (class of title)

cuts.event: Court of Appeal: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2 dismisses the appeal. Possession in six weeks; leave to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
cuts.blow: The licence-by-letter reasoning became binding law, and ownership itself was never decided. The court accepted that Frederick and Mary were in adverse possession from 1955, but held that the 1962 order and the 1974 letters defeated it.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: Petition for leave to appeal to the House of Lords.
cuts.blow: The last domestic route closed.
cuts.label: Record (petition); outcome papers not yet held

cuts.event: Application to the European Commission of Human Rights (14464/88), later declared inadmissible.
cuts.blow: The international route closed without a hearing on the merits.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: First eviction attempt. BP's spokesman explains the case to the press; the family are publicly framed as people with no right to be there.
cuts.blow: In public the family became occupiers resisting bailiffs, the "squatters" label others applied, rather than a family with an undecided ownership plea.
cuts.label: Record (press); the label is others', not ours

cuts.event: Estates Gazette: "BP signal Welsh sales".
cuts.blow: Our reading: the site was now an asset for sale, which gave a motive to clear it. Nothing yet ties the 1982–83 filings to this sale.
cuts.label: Record (press); our reading (motive)

cuts.event: Cadw inspects and photographs the house; the listing decision comes in December 1988.
cuts.blow: The heritage protection that might have saved the house came too late to stop the demolition.
cuts.label: Record

cuts.event: Forced entry and the outbuilding roof removed; the residents are evicted; Mr Buckler is taken from a hospital bed to face an assault charge.
cuts.blow: The physical removal of the family. The charge put the son in the dock rather than BP.
cuts.label: Record (press)

cuts.event: The final eviction hearing in the Cardiff High Court fails.
cuts.blow: The last court door closed on the day before the demolition.
cuts.label: Record (press)

cuts.event: The farmhouse is demolished ("Tears flow as 800 year-old farm house is razed at last").
cuts.blow: The apex. With the house gone there was nothing left to occupy, list or restore. The Sites and Monuments Record later entered: "building destroyed by owners".
cuts.label: Record (press, SMR)

epilogue.event: Vale councillors authorise legal action against BP Properties over the demolition.
Sites and Monuments Record PRN 02038s: "building destroyed by owners".
Outline planning permission for houses at Great House Farm (89/01396/OUT).
Reserved matters approved and 20 houses built.

reading: Our reading: across 39 cuts from 1916 to 1988 the family's standing was cut down piece by piece: first as tenants (1916, 1949), then as occupiers under a court order (1955, 1962), then as licensees by letter (1974), then as occupiers of land registered to someone else (1983), and finally as people removed by force (1988).

None of these steps decided who owned the house. The 1974 ownership plea was adjourned part-heard and "has never been finally heard". The 1986 and 1987 courts decided possession and limitation, not the family's ownership plea.
So, on our reading, the family's rights were diminished step by step, but their ownership claim was never tested on its merits and never extinguished by any decision on it.

The outcome was eviction, demolition, no compensation and no finding against anyone. Presenting that as settled and fair rests on these cuts, not on a decision about ownership. That is the moral point of this page, and we put it as our reading, not as a finding.
confirm: The 1974 Cardiff County Court file, including the part-heard action and the leave application (HMCTS reply due 2 Nov 2026), would show what was pleaded and what was never decided.
The Land Registry's 1983 application papers and the 8 Apr, 12 Apr and 12 May 1983 letters (subject access request due 28 Oct 2026) would show what BP told the Registry about who lived in the house.
A letter from Mary or her solicitors after 31 Oct 1974 rejecting the licence would meet the exact point the Court of Appeal said might have changed the result.
The 1938 Bute–Western Ground Rents conveyance and plan would show whether the farmhouse parcel was ever in the paper chain.
against: The courts found the opposite on the points they decided. The Court of Appeal held that the 1962 order stopped the clock before 12 years had run, and that from the 1974 letters her possession was no longer adverse. Both points bind unless a ground to reopen is made out.
The judgment records rent arrears in the 1930s and 1940s and a last payment in 1953. That is against the family's 1928 account.

The Court of Appeal did accept that Frederick and Mary were in adverse possession from 1955. The loss came from the order and the letters, not from any finding that the family never possessed as owners.
BP did not need the 1983 registration to sue. It sued in May 1984 and won on the 1974 letters.
No record yet shows BP knew of Mary's final illness, or that the 1983 filing was timed to it.
Several peak items (Marconi's stay, Driscoll's fight, the 1928 receipt) are family testimony or not yet confirmed.

act1983: Which 1983 Act: the Commons Registration (Glamorgan) Act 1983 (c. ix; Royal Assent 26 Jul 1983, in force 1 Sep 1983), EV-0232. It is the only 1983 statute our research has read and catalogued for the farm. Our reading is that it did not reach the farmhouse or VG41 directly, so it is listed as a cut with that counter-note. If the 1983 step meant is BP's 1983 registration of the farmhouse, that is cuts C25 and C27.
labels_note: Record = read in a court judgment, registry, archive, legislation or contemporaneous press. Family testimony = the family's own account. Our reading = interpretation. Not yet confirmed = no source located yet.
